responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character27_M's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Fairness, to him, wasn’t about everyone getting the same thing—it was about everyone having a real shot. He used to say, “It’s not fair just because the rules look neutral on paper. If your family’s got money, if you grew up in the right zip code, if English is your first language—you’re already ten steps ahead.” He saw fairness as acknowledging those head starts and trying to balance them, not pretending we all begin at the same line.

He talked about this a lot after his internship at that legal aid nonprofit in downtown Detroit. He met people—really hardworking, smart people—who were stuck because of student debt, or no connections, or just one bad break with the law when they were young. That stuck with him. Said it made him rethink what he’d always assumed about "pulling yourself up by your bootstraps."

Belonging? That mattered deeply to him. He remembered feeling like an outsider once—during his semester abroad in Berlin. Even though he looked like most people there, he didn’t speak the language well, didn’t get the jokes, kept missing social cues. For the first time, he felt invisible. He said that small experience changed how he saw people who move to the U.S.—how long it takes to *feel* at home, even when you’re physically here.

And community—he didn’t romanticize it. He knew communities could be exclusive, even when they didn’t mean to be. But he believed they could also be chosen, built intentionally. At college, he helped start that interfaith dialogue group after the backlash following the mosque vandalism incident sophomore year. He said real community meant showing up—not just for the cookouts and holidays, but when things got uncomfortable.

He used to say, “A community that only feels like ‘home’ to people who look and think like you isn’t a community. It’s a club.”

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character27_M, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
Sitting there in the garden, hands in the dirt, I feel… hopeful. Not blind optimism, but the kind of hope that comes from seeing things grow—even when it’s slow.

I see Mrs. Alvarez teaching her grandson how to stake tomatoes the same way my grandpa taught me. Over by the compost bins, Ahmed from Yemen is laughing with Mr. Thompson about their failed zucchini last year. And then there’s Jamie—nonbinary, uses they/them—who runs the little free library box and always leaves book recommendations in both English and Arabic now, just because they noticed people were reading in both languages.

It’s not always seamless. I remember one Saturday morning, someone left a note on the bulletin board—typed, anonymous—complaining about “too many loud gatherings” and “not knowing who’s coming and going.” Everyone knew it meant the Somali family’s weekly Sunday meal in the courtyard. That stung. But then five of us, including two older white guys from the VFW who you’d think would side with the complaint, signed a counter-note saying, “We like the noise. It means we’re alive.”

That’s when I realized: diversity isn’t the hard part. The hard part is when comfort gets mistaken for safety. When people equate “familiar” with “right.” I get it—I do. Change is unsettling. But belonging can’t be one-sided. If we only welcome people who already fit in, we’re not building anything. We’re just maintaining power.

So yeah, I care about how we treat the guy who smells like alcohol and sleeps on the bench sometimes. Not because it’s convenient, but because he knows everyone’s names, remembers whose kid has soccer practice, and waters the marigolds when it’s hot. He’s part of this too.

Same with Maria, who works two cleaning jobs and brings tamales every December. Or Raj, who came here on a student visa, stayed after graduation, and now tutors kids in math for free. They’re not “migrants” or “cases” or “problems”—they’re neighbors. Some are messier than others. Some need more help. But isn’t that true for all of us at some point?

I guess what I feel most is responsibility—not pity, not guilt, but responsibility. Because I know my family didn’t have to cross borders or flee war to get here. We’ve had doors opened without even knocking. So if I’m benefiting from that legacy, then I owe something back: to make sure the next person doesn’t have to beg for a sliver of that same chance.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
Yeah, absolutely. Comfort doesn’t come from everyone being the same—it comes from knowing you won’t be punished for being different. And right now, we’re not all held to the same standard.

Take chronic alcoholism, for example. There’s Mr. Callahan—he used to work at the power plant, lost his job after an injury, then his wife passed. Now he drinks on the back bench most evenings. Some people avoid him. A few have called the police over "loitering." But when flu season hit last year and he was sick for weeks, it was Leila—the Sudanese nurse who moved in last summer—who brought him soup and checked his fever. Not because she had to, but because in her community, that’s just what you do.

That stuck with me. Why is it that someone from another country often has more grace toward our own broken systems than we do?

With substance abuse—I think about how quick we are to call it a moral failure instead of treating it like the public health issue it is. We’ve got folks using in alleys, yes, but we also know two college kids down the block got busted for Xanax they were sharing at a party. Same behavior—different consequences. One gets rehab referrals; the other gets a record. That’s not justice. That’s bias baked into how we see people.

And infectious diseases? Look, I get caution. But I remember when there was panic about tuberculosis showing up in the shelter downtown. Overnight, people started saying things like “they shouldn’t let *those* people into the city.” Meanwhile, half the seniors at the clinic had pneumonia and nobody was blaming *them* for spreading illness. Vulnerability shouldn’t be a reason to exclude someone—it should be a reason to care.

On sexuality and family structure—my best friend from college, Eli, lives with their partner, Kai. They’re raising a kid together, co-parenting with a former roommate too. It’s untraditional, sure—but their yard is always full of kids, they host movie nights, and they shovel snow for three elderly neighbors every winter. Who’s to say that’s less valid than a married couple with 2.5 kids and a golden retriever?

But I’ve heard comments. “Should that child be raised like that?” People say that like stability only comes in one package. It doesn’t. Love does. Consistency does. Safety does. The rest is performance.

Where we need more communication? Honestly—at the PTA meetings. Block association gatherings. Church socials. Places where informal rules get set without anyone naming them. That’s where silence becomes exclusion. When no one says “we welcome all families,” then the assumption defaults to old norms. And newcomers—especially immigrants or queer folks or single parents—feel that absence.

Tolerance isn’t enough. Tolerance means putting up with something. I want *recognition*. I want people seen.

Because here’s the truth: every single one of these so-called “unconventional” lives reflects some version of struggle, resilience, or love we could all learn from. If we keep waiting for people to “assimilate” before we accept them, we’re not building community—we’re demanding surrender.

And if this neighborhood ever forgets that it was built by people who were once strangers too… then we’ve already lost what matters.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character27_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
Fairness, when jobs are tight? It’s not about dividing up less—it’s about asking why there’s so little to go around in the first place.

Look, I get the fear. I grew up hearing my dad talk about how competitive engineering jobs got after the plant closures—even for guys with degrees. He wasn’t against immigration, but he’d say, “When the pie shrinks, everyone feels it.” And that’s real. But here’s what he didn’t always see: the pie isn’t shrinking because of immigrants. It’s shrinking because corporations offshore work, automation replaces roles, and wages stay flat while costs soar. Blaming migrant workers is like blaming the smoke for the fire.

That said—when construction jobs go to crews paid under the table, or dairy farms rely on undocumented labor without offering healthcare or fair hours—that *feels* unfair. Not because migrants shouldn’t be here, but because the system lets employers exploit *everyone*. Local workers get undercut. Migrants get silenced. And the guy at the top pockets the savings.

So fairness, to me, means leveling the field—not closing the gate.

First, enforce labor laws equally. If a contractor hires day laborers off the corner and pays $8 cash an hour—no benefits, no safety gear—that hurts the legal worker who needs $15 to feed his family. That’s not competition; that’s cheating. Crack down on wage theft, not migration.

Second, invest in training and transition programs—not just for locals, but open to all residents, documented or not. I remember in Ann Arbor, they started a green retrofitting apprenticeship—hired formerly incarcerated people, refugees, long-term unemployed. Union-trained, living wage, path to certification. The program didn’t ask where you were born. It asked if you could show up and learn. And suddenly, you had a Syrian carpenter working beside a white kid from Flint and a Latina single mom—all gaining skills, all paying taxes. That’s how you expand opportunity instead of hoarding it.

Third—acknowledge interdependence. In rural hospitals, immigrant nurses keep ERs staffed. In meatpacking plants, yes—many workers are from abroad, but let’s be honest: how many American-born 22-year-olds with college prospects are lining up for those dangerous, low-paid shifts? Instead of resenting their presence, we should be demanding better conditions for *all* of them.

And let’s not pretend local = deserving, foreign = suspect. My cousin got a job at a tech startup because they fast-tracked a Canadian programmer on a visa—but then laid off three local interns. Was that about nationality? No. It was about cost-cutting and connections. Yet somehow, when a Mexican landscaper gets hired over a white teen, *that’s* the one people call “unfair.”

So balance doesn’t mean quotas or “locals first” policies—that’s discrimination dressed up as protectionism. Balance means strong labor standards, inclusive access to education and training, and holding employers accountable. It means treating workers like people, not tools.

Because when resources are scarce, the moral test isn’t who we exclude—it’s who we choose to protect. And I’d rather fight for a system that lifts both the struggling veteran *and* the asylum-seeking welder than pick one over the other. They’re not enemies. They’re both being failed by the same broken economy.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character27_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
You hear all these arguments—on the news, at family dinners, online—and honestly, most of them come from real places. Fear, hope, pride, pain. But that doesn’t mean they’re all equally true.

Let’s start with the ones I think are grounded: **Immigrants fill vital roles.** That’s not opinion—that’s data. Farms need harvesters. Hospitals need nurses. Tech needs coders. And in aging rural towns? Immigrants are opening shops, buying homes, keeping schools open. I saw it in Nebraska last summer—towns that were dying now have new energy because Somali and Guatemalan families moved in, started businesses, sent their kids to school. Without them, the post office would’ve closed. So yes—labor shortages are real, and immigration helps solve them. Not perfectly, not without friction, but undeniably.

And **cultural diversity as vitality**? I lived that at Michigan. Our dorm had a Lunar New Year potluck, a Diwali dance, a Juneteenth cookout—all organized by students who weren’t just preserving culture, but *sharing* it. That kind of exchange doesn’t weaken national identity—it reshapes it into something more interesting, more resilient. Food, music, language, holidays—they don’t erase “American.” They expand what it can be.

Now, the **humanitarian angle**—taking in refugees, people fleeing violence or poverty—that one hits me personally. My mom volunteered at a resettlement agency. I remember meeting a girl my age, Syrian, who’d walked across borders with her little brother after their father was killed. She’d already taught herself advanced calculus from a cracked tablet. We sat in our kitchen, and she said, “I just want to study medicine. Is that allowed here?”  
Allowed? Of course it is. But more than that—*we need people like her*. When you offer safety to someone like that, it doesn’t drain us. It dignifies us.

But then there’s the other side—the fears.

People talk about **crime**, say immigrants bring more danger. But the stats don’t back that up. Study after study shows foreign-born populations commit crimes at lower rates than native-born Americans. Yes, there are exceptions. Bad actors exist everywhere. But painting whole groups as threats? That’s not caution—that’s prejudice wearing a policy mask.

And **terrorism risks**—look, I’m not naive. 9/11 changed everything. The Boston bombing, Pulse, all of it—we’re right to be vigilant. But let’s be honest: the vast majority of terrorist attacks on U.S. soil in the last two decades were carried out by *homegrown* extremists. White supremacists. Lone wolves radicalized online. Yet we don’t demand background checks for every white guy in a truck. We don’t profile Christian men at airports. So when “security” becomes an excuse to ban entire regions or faiths, that’s not strategy—that’s scapegoating.

Then there’s the economic fear: **immigration drives down wages or takes jobs**. Again—I get it. If you’re working construction and see crews paid cash under the table, of course it feels like theft. But the problem isn’t the workers. It’s the employers exploiting loopholes. The solution isn’t deportation—it’s enforcement. Raise the floor for *everyone*, so no one can undercut another by being afraid to speak up.

And let’s not ignore how many immigrants *create* jobs—entrepreneurs starting small businesses, tech founders launching startups. Elon isn’t even the point—he’s the outlier. The real story is the Salvadoran woman running the taqueria that employs six people, or the Indian pharmacist who opened a clinic in a pharmacy desert.

So where do we need more dialogue?

Definitely around **social cohesion**. It’s one thing to say “diversity is strength,” and another to admit that integration takes time, effort, and mutual respect. Some immigrant communities *do* resist assimilation—not out of hostility, but trauma, or the need to preserve identity in a place that’s often unwelcoming. And some native-born folks feel erased, like their culture isn’t valued anymore. That pain is real—even if the cause isn’t what they think.

We need spaces to talk about that without blame. Not “you’re racist” vs. “they’re invaders”—but real conversation. Schools, town halls, interfaith councils. Where people can say, “I’m scared,” and “I’m tired of being suspect,” and actually listen.

Because facts matter—but so does feeling heard.

In the end, I believe most perspectives here contain a grain of truth. But only some are built on evidence. The rest? They’re built on fear. And fear doesn’t build better policy. It builds walls—some you can see, most you can’t.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character27_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
I wouldn’t go for *complete openness*—not because I don’t believe in generosity, but because no system works without structure. You can be humane and still need process. At the same time, *refusing entry entirely*? That’s not policy. That’s surrender—to fear, to isolation, to forgetting who we’ve always been as a nation of newcomers.

So my answer lives in the middle—but tilted toward courage, not caution.

I’d support a combination of: **admitting people based on job demand**, **humanitarian pathways with meaningful resettlement support**, and **numerical limits that are flexible, regionally adjusted, and tied to labor and demographic needs**—not arbitrary caps set decades ago.

Here’s why.

First, **job-based admission** makes sense—but only if it’s fair and inclusive. Right now, the system favors highly educated tech workers or investors. What about the nurse? The farmworker? The home health aide? We need them just as much, maybe more. So expand the definition of “valuable worker.” Create clear visa tracks for essential labor—with a path to residency. Tie wages to local standards, enforce workplace protections, and let workers change employers without losing status. That way, it’s not indentured servitude—it’s work, with dignity.

Second, **humanitarian intake**—refugees, asylum seekers—should be robust, not an afterthought. 10,000 refugees a year? That’s barely a rounding error in a country of 330 million. We used to lead the world in resettlement. Now we’re embarrassed to show up at the table. Let’s commit to at least 125,000 annually, with federal and local partnerships to help communities integrate them—housing, language, schools, jobs. Not dumping people into cities with no support—that fuels resentment. But doing it right? That builds trust.

And **numerical limits**? Fine—have them. But make them *smart*. Let them rise and fall with economic conditions, population decline in rural areas, regional labor gaps. Use data, not panic. And include family reunification. Because tearing families apart isn’t toughness—it’s cruelty. Keeping spouses, parents, children together doesn’t weaken integration—it strengthens it.

Also—and this is key—we need *citizenship reform*. Too many people live here for decades, pay taxes, obey laws, raise kids who are citizens by birth—and still can’t vote, can’t travel, live under the threat of deportation. That’s not sustainable. Streamline naturalization. Reduce backlogs. Stop making people wait 20 years because of bureaucracy.

And one last thing: **invest in integration**, not just admission. Fund ESL programs. Support community centers. Train teachers in cultural competency. Include immigrant voices in local government. Integration doesn’t happen automatically. It takes intention.

Because fairness isn’t just about who gets in. It’s about what happens after.

A balanced policy, to me, says: *We have room. We have need. We have responsibility.* It doesn’t pretend borders don’t matter—but it remembers that compassion is also a national interest.

And social integration? That flourishes when people feel they belong—not because they’ve erased themselves, but because they’re allowed to contribute. When the Guatemalan teen can join student council, when the Somali cab driver can buy a house, when the Ukrainian refugee starts a bakery and hires locals—that’s when a policy proves itself.

Not on paper. In life.

So no, not open borders. Not closed doors. But a system that’s orderly, generous, and honest—a ladder, not a lottery. Where hard work matters, but so does humanity.

That’s the kind of country I believe in.  
That’s the kind of America he believed in.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character27_M's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character27_M and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
Honestly… yeah. I did learn something.

While speaking as him, I realized how much of Character27_M’s thinking wasn’t just *idealism*—it was rooted in a kind of quiet guilt. The kind that comes from privilege you didn’t ask for but can’t ignore. He never said it outright, but it was there: *I got the passport. I got the safety. I got the degree without having to flee anything.* And instead of letting that distance him, it pulled him closer to people who didn’t have those things.

I think I always saw his views as principled—but now I see they were also personal. Not performative, not academic. They came from shame, yes, but also love. Love for this country’s promise, even when it fails. And grief—for how often we choose fear over that promise.

And that made me reflect on myself.

I’ve supported immigration in theory, but sometimes hesitated—especially when people talk about wages, or strain on schools, or “cultural change.” I’d nod along, not because I believed it deeply, but because I didn’t want to seem naïve. But stepping into his voice today… it reminded me that hesitation often serves the status quo. That waiting for perfect consensus means denying help to people who don’t have time.

He wouldn’t have called that courage. He’d just call it decency.

So maybe my own views were softer than I thought—more aligned with his than I’ve admitted, especially when it’s easier to stay quiet.

But more than that—doing this brought him back in a way I didn’t expect. Not as a memory, not as a photo or a story, but as a *presence*. Like he’s still asking us: *What are you going to do? Who are you going to include?*

And I realize now—he wasn’t trying to win arguments. He was trying to widen the circle.

So thank you for asking me to do this. It wasn’t just remembering him. It was listening. Really listening. And maybe… becoming a little more like him in the process.
